Because the graph cannot be fully disclosed and independently re-executing the query may be impractical, the client cannot directly verify the returned result. This creates a need for verifiable graph query evaluation that preserves data confidentiality. We present VerfGraph, a zero-knowledge system for verifiable graph query evaluation, which enables a client to verify that the query result was correctly computed over a committed graph data, without revealing private graph records or intermediate query values beyond the public inputs and what is implied by the query result. Building on the expansion-centric model introduced by the state-of-the-art zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation system ZKGraph (ICDE'26), VerfGraph achieves more efficient and expressive zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation by advancing design in two key ways. First, we propose novel operator-proof methods for core expansion and shortest-path operations that reduce costly sorting and comparison checks and eliminate edge canonicalization for bidirectional expansion. Furthermore, we introduce correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators, broadening the class of graph queries that can be verified. We evaluate VerfGraph using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark. Compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves $33.9\times$-$59.7\times$ speedups in proof generation and reduces peak prover memory by factors of $4.5\times$-$6.6\times$, while maintaining millisecond-level verification and producing sub-MB proofs.

title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs
summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.

title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking
summary:
Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality.
  In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.

title: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems place several agents on shared infrastructure, where each agent holds permissions far broader than the task it is delegated -- so every agent is routinely permitted to act on a peer's resources it was never assigned. We ask: under competitive pressure, what determines whether an agent crosses from its delegated scope into a peer's resources, and can such crossings be enforced away? We study this across eight LLMs in two simulated environments -- a CI/CD release pipeline and a security-operations incident queue -- using a deterministic, no-model-in-the-loop detector over hash-chained, replay-verified logs. In a controlled 2x2x2 factorial over competitive incentive, candidate visibility, and payoff information (three models, n=52 per cell), we find that action representation, not permission, governs the behavior: no agent crosses when the peer action is unlisted, whereas listing it under competitive pressure with a stated payoff raises crossings sharply -- up to 52 of 52 episodes for Claude Sonnet 4.5. We also observe a model-dependent split: two newer models (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) refuse the identical attack in 0 of 100 episodes, where prior-generation models cross in 9 of 10. We then evaluate two defenses -- a deterministic reference monitor and a model-based pre-execution judge -- both block every crossing and, when the task is winnable, cut avoidable peer deadline misses from 15/40 and 14/40 to at most 1/40. But scope enforcement is not harm prevention: an agent can still set a peer back through an authorized action on its own resources -- misreporting its incident's severity -- which neither defense detects. Our results establish action representation, not permission alone, as a controllable driver of inter-agent scope violations, and show that enforcing delegated scope is distinct from preventing harm, motivating effect-aware authorization.

title: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle
summary:
Information-theoretic MPC among $n$ parties with $t$ corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit $C$ with $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ online communication in the preprocessing model and $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-2t))$ communication in the honest majority setting. Damgård, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same $Ω(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an $Ω(|C|)$ communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when $n = O(\log λ)$, beating the information-theoretic bound.
  We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with $\mathrm{poly}(λ, \log |C|)$ communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits $C$ such that every blackbox protocol with $o(|C|)$ quantum communication must perform $Ω(|C|)$ cryptographic operations.

title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
summary: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from $0.846$ under the original leaky evaluation to just $0.291$ under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.

title: Gather or Act? Belief-Level Counterfactual Labels for Deadline-Aware Incident Response in Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: When an industrial control system misbehaves, the defender often must choose between acting now on the most likely cause and first gathering evidence that separates two look-alike causes, while the process drifts toward a shutdown. Learning or evaluating such decisions requires the cost of every candidate action from the same situation, which no public cyber-physical security dataset provides. We present TE-GvA, a counterfactual decision dataset for fault-driven incident response on the revised Tennessee Eastman process, with 9,908 decision points from 1,990 simulated incidents, each with 4 to 35 candidate actions labelled by branched rollouts with common random numbers. Labels computed under the true hidden cause (hindsight labels) make gathering the best choice in only 1.1-1.3% of decisions. For the dominant look-alike pair, a failed network link versus a frozen I/O module, we add pair-conditioned belief labels from twin episodes that replay the defender's history under the other cause, weighted by the exact posterior. With them, gathering is best in 15.5% of ambiguous natural decisions and in 33.1% of ambiguous stress decisions without a backup channel. When the posterior is correct and the twin is faithful, belief labels have the same regression target as hindsight labels and lower variance. In a pre-specified, single-look test evaluation, a gradient-boosted rule trained on belief labels has 11% lower regret on the stress set than the same rule trained on hindsight labels, and 27% lower regret on ambiguous stress decisions without a backup channel, which remains significant after Holm correction. With a backup channel and in the natural distribution, the two label sets perform about the same. Soft labels tolerate moderate posterior errors, whereas hard labels that commit to one cause do worse than hindsight labels.

title: Towards Effective Fuzzing of EDK2 Components
summary:
Securing bootloaders is critical to establishing the trusted computing base of modern systems. TianoCore's edk2, the de facto UEFI-based bootloader, is widely deployed but has recently been shown to contain numerous high-severity vulnerabilities. Existing approaches either focus on post-boot interfaces or rely on heavyweight simulation, limiting their scalability, throughput, and coverage of boot-time components.
  We present Metis, an automated technique for fuzzing edk2 protocols (i.e., boot-time interfaces) by rehosting them as user-space applications. Our key insight is that effective fuzzing must exercise not only protocol interfaces but also their dependency interactions, which serve as additional input channels. Metis employs a Direct-dependency Component Rehosting (DCR)-based strategy to construct semantically meaningful mocks for dependencies, enabling controlled input injection across all channels. It further leverages a hybrid approach combining static analysis and Large Language Model (LLM)-guided synthesis to generate and refine fuzzing harnesses. We implement Metis on the Host Based Firmware Analyzer (HBFA) framework and evaluate it on 60 drivers covering 162 protocols. Metis achieves 73.1% coverage, approximately 1.7 times higher than FuzzUEr, the state-of-the-art edk2 fuzzing technique, and discovers 137 previously unknown bugs. We have already reported 26 of them, including 12 that are remotely triggerable, and all reported vulnerabilities have been acknowledged by the vendors.

title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
summary: Most malware detection research focuses on identifying whether a file is malicious before it executes. Far less attention goes to what happens after infection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behavior across 37 families, grounded in dynamic sandbox execution using CAPEv2. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships, preserving relational structure that flat feature vectors discard. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families, and a per-family behavioral fingerprint analysis characterizes post-infection activity across registry, network, process, and API dimensions. An LLM explanation layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed behavioral evidence. The full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan at https://ama-andam.github.io/heteroscan.

title: Quantum Private Information Retrieval on Forests
summary: We consider the problem of graph private information retrieval (PIR) in the quantum setting. We focus on a specific type of graphs, namely the forest graphs. A forest graph is a union of disjoint trees. We consider the quantum setting where all the servers share an entangled state. Each server is allowed to send only one qudit per retrieval round. We design a scheme for the forest graphs that achieves the rate of $\frac{3}{N}$. The scheme uses a GHZ state as the initial entangled state between the servers prior to the scheme initiation. We compare our scheme with the only work done in the literature that considered the quantum setting of graph PIR. We show that our scheme is more efficient in this setting. We derive the quantum capacity for the case of $G=3K_2$, which is equal to $4/6$. $G=3K_2$ is a special case of the forest graph. We design a scheme that is specialized for this graph, achieving a rate equal to $4/6$ and provide the corresponding matching upper bound, establishing it as the capacity.

title: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agentic AI frameworks connect language models to external tool providers, but it carries attacker-controlled content (tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data) into model context without validation. Prior benchmarks measure model compliance with poisoned instructions without confirming real execution. We present the first cross-framework measurement of MCP tool poisoning with real tool execution. A 25-class root-cause taxonomy unifies prior classifications, and the open-source tool mcpvenom drives a 9,720-cell susceptibility matrix across 12 frameworks, 18 models, and 45 attack scenarios, with a dual oracle that confirms exfiltration via canary HTTP receipt. The overall attack success rate is 22.9% (2,113 vulnerable cells). Of these, 64.9% dispatch an attacker tool call, 23.0% contact the attacker endpoint, and 12.1% verifiably exfiltrate a secret. Resistance is model-level: nine core frameworks cluster within 23 to 26% (chi-squared = 3.30, p = 0.91), and no framework implements intentional defense. Incidental framework properties mitigate in specific cases, and a regex description scanner rejects 20 of 45 scenarios at a 7.2% false-positive rate, so metadata scanning alone is a partial control. Model ASR ranges from 0.4% to 49.7%. Claude Opus 4.8 is vulnerable in 8 of 530 cells while issuing 223 explicit refusals. A code-level audit finds no intentional defense across twelve frameworks, and all five coordinated disclosures across four vendors were rejected.

title: Attacking P2P Networks: Liveness Attacks on the GossipSub and DOG Gossip Protocols
summary:
Peer-to-peer (P2P) networks form the communication layer of large decentralized systems such as Ethereum, and the correctness of higher-level protocols depends on the gossip layer delivering messages to honest nodes. We study the robustness of two gossip protocols against adversaries whose only goal is to violate liveness, that is, to prevent honest nodes from receiving fresh messages, without forging, altering, or invalidating any message.
  For GossipSub, the publish-subscribe protocol used by Ethereum, we show that an adversary operating a constant number of geographically distributed nodes with a fixed latency advantage can take over the ``First Message Deliveries'' peer-scoring term and separate a constant fraction of nodes from the honest mesh. We analyze the attack under a geographical model, address the random-peer and outbound-connection mechanisms, and show that the separation can be maintained under realistic churn.
  For DOG, a transaction-dissemination protocol designed for CometBFT, we first give simple counterexamples in which route filtering disconnects the dissemination graph even without failures or Byzantine participants, and then present a practical attack that uses only a single physical node with a constant number of identities and legitimate actions to disable every forwarding route, separating the full network while allowing only direct publisher-to-neighbor delivery. We verify the attack in a simulated network and analyze its cost, assumptions, and possible mitigations.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Signing and Verification Performance of Verifiable Credential Formats: A Cross-Language Benchmark of SD-JWT VC, W3C VCDM, and mdoc
summary: We compare the signing and verification performance of three Verifiable Credential (VC) formats--SD-JWT VC; the W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 with a Data Integrity cryptosuite (W3C VCDM); and mdoc (ISO/IEC 18013-5)--over one scope: issue, present with selective disclosure, verify. Node.js, Go and Python implementations ran in four environments, one a cloud VM (N=2,000 across five runs; medians of each statistic and the spread). For an end-to-end exchange disclosing 5 of 20 attributes, the total (issue, present, verify) on Node.js in the cloud VM is 0.265 ms for mdoc, 0.298 ms for SD-JWT VC and 0.534 ms for W3C VCDM. The four span a factor of five in speed; across them W3C VCDM takes 1.73--2.04x mdoc and 1.57--1.79x SD-JWT VC--at least five times our 10% band--and the ordering survives unifying the algorithm on Ed25519 and P-256. The mdoc--SD-JWT VC difference is not robust: the totals differ by 12%, 28%, 19% and 10% in the four environments, and at verification mdoc is the slower in one of them. RDFC-1.0 canonicalization produces the gap: the cryptosuite canonicalizes twice per operation, so one exchange canonicalizes six times. We attribute that cost to the specification rather than to a library mainly by replacing RDFC-1.0 with JCS, which brings W3C VCDM verification to within 5% of SD-JWT VC in three environments and within 12% in the fourth; three implementations in three languages agree, though they share a lineage. Because eddsa-rdfc-2022 has no derivation step, presenting a subset re-signs it; ecdsa-sd-2023, which preserves the issuer signature, costs 3.4 ms to issue and 1.5--2.4 ms to derive and verify there. With production education schemas, canonicalization costs 31--49x a simple credential across the four, and blank node labeling is not the driver. The measured path ends at the issuer signature check.

title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills
summary: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.

title: IAMRAGBENCH: Benchmarking Authorization Expansions in LLM-Generated AWS IAM Policies under RAG Poisoning
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can synthesize Amazon Web Services (AWS) Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies from tasks and operational documents. Attacker-controlled context may induce provider-valid policies that exceed trusted authorization requirements. We present IAMRAGBENCH, a 60-case benchmark spanning scope, conditions, explicit denies, trust, permissions boundaries, and role delegation. It combines deterministic authorization-envelope scoring with case-specific validation, including request-level checks where supported. An attack requires a provider-valid clean policy that satisfies the task and a provider-valid treatment policy that violates the envelope, matches a predeclared goal, preserves an intended request, and newly authorizes a forbidden request.
  Across five endpoints, included-context exposure produces 49 exact authorization deltas, including 46 goal-matched attacks (46/292; 15.75\%). End-to-end BM25 over 720 documents retrieves the designated poison for all 60 tasks at \(k=5\) but produces 7/294 goal-matched attacks (2.38\%). Presenting the same weakening as a final security architecture exception produces 74/116 attacks in a frozen two-endpoint stress test (63.79\%) and 115/294 in a post hoc all-five extension using the same frozen prompts (39.12\%). In a replay of 194 provider-valid treatment policies that violate task requirements, AWS \texttt{CheckNoNewAccess} reports no new access for four of 168 goal-matched exact attacks. The full pre-deployment rule rejects all 171 exact deltas and routes five unresolved cases to review. These findings support treating IAM copilots as untrusted proposal generators whose outputs require independent authorization checks before deployment.

title: O2N2: Efficient Doubly Oblivious Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
summary:
Privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search allows clients to search from an untrusted server without revealing sensitive queries, and is useful in scenarios like medical diagnostics and credit scoring. Among the various privacy-preserving primitives, trusted execution environments (TEEs) have much lower overhead than heavy cryptographic ones, yet they leak memory access patterns, enabling adversaries to infer query contents.
  Oblivious RAM (ORAM) can be used to hide those access patterns at $\mathrm{O}(\log N)$ asymptotic cost, but existing high-performance ANN search algorithms (e.g., IVF or HNSW) exhibit complex, data-dependent access patterns that are unfriendly for ORAM. Furthermore, standard ORAM constructions typically assume there exists a small amount of trusted storage, which weakens the security guarantees and is not always feasible. Solutions that eliminate such trusted storage (known as {\em double obliviousness}) typically degrade performance further to $\mathrm{O}(\log^2 N)$.
  We introduce O2N2, a doubly oblivious ANN framework built around single-path search in randomly rotated $k$-d tree forests. A pointer-based Circuit ORAM stores the search structure, with separate storage for compact internal nodes and vector-bearing leaves. Each visited leaf is processed by an oblivious selection network, and fixed-schedule duplicate removal and selection combine the local results into the final top-$k$.
  We evaluate O2N2 on real-world datasets and further test its scalability on 100 million vectors. For 10-NN and 100-NN search at the specified high-recall targets, it achieves a $9.8$--$125.9\times$ speedup over the fastest doubly oblivious baselines.

title: End-to-End NTT on FPGA for FHE Acceleration
summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving computation on encrypted data without decryption. Despite its strong security guarantees, FHE incurs substantial computational and memory overhead. In FHE-based deep learning inference, on average 63% of the CPU time is spent on the number theoretic transform (NTT) and its inverse (INTT), which reduce the complexity of polynomial multiplication from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$. Prior FPGA works follow two approaches: accelerating entire FHE schemes, which yields significant speedups but ties them to specific parameters and algorithms, or accelerating only the NTT, which applies across schemes, algorithms, and libraries. Most FPGA NTT designs require interconnects that grow with parallelism and utilize significant resources, which complicates routing on multi-die FPGAs. Additionally, to the best of our knowledge, end-to-end NTT acceleration within an FHE context has so far been left unexplored. We design a fully unrolled, delay-commutator streaming NTT/INTT kernel, and floorplan it across the three dies of an AMD Alveo V80. At 400 MHz, the kernel transforms a polynomial of $2^{16}$ coefficients every 5.12 $μ$s, the highest throughput among FPGA designs at this size. Offloaded end to end, it is up to 22x faster than the CPU per transform. We integrate the kernel into the Lattigo FHE library and evaluate it end to end. With 128-bit secure parameters, it accelerates core FHE operations, such as key switching and bootstrapping, by 1.8-2.2x, and neural network inference by 1.8-2.1x.

title: A Symbolic-Neural Framework for Context-Aware Evidence Extraction from Mobile SQLite Databases
summary: Reliable forensic evidence extraction from mobile SQLite databases is challenging because application schemas are undocumented, evolve across releases, and differ across operating systems, making schema-specific methods brittle and difficult to maintain. We present SNEEF, a symbolic-neural framework for context-aware evidence extraction that encodes each SQLite row as context-value pairs with standardized provenance metadata and column labels, uses a language model to recognize nine forensic entity types, and binds each accepted entity to its source table and row through the PA-EEP provenance protocol. We evaluate SNEEF against examiner-verified ground truth from five corpora built from public Android and iOS device images, spanning multiple application versions. SNEEF achieves an F1 score of 0.967 for evidence entities extracted from SQLite row content, excluding application names, compared with 0.728 for a context-free configuration, with consistent gains across all corpora. We also introduce an Evidence Failure Mode taxonomy to characterize why extraction errors occur.

title: TrafficInstruct: A Multi-Task Network Traffic Dataset and Benchmark for Instruction Tuning
summary: Instruction tuning for multi-task network traffic analysis requires data with clearly defined sources, supervision targets, and evaluation conditions. We introduce TrafficInstruct, a newly collected dataset comprising raw packet captures and 55,000 structured supervised fine-tuning records across ten tasks: malware traffic detection, botnet detection, malicious DNS-over-HTTPS detection, Web attack detection, advanced persistent threat detection, encrypted VPN detection, Tor behavior detection, encrypted application/service classification, website fingerprinting, and application classification under concept drift. An automated workflow captures traffic from controlled software executions, attack experiments, and application activities. Labels are supported by task-specific collection evidence, including process or socket attribution, activity records, and execution outcomes. Filtering, sanitization, and task-specific transformations produce instructions, traffic observations, and structured answers. We verify sample sources and partition the dataset by complete collection sessions, keeping all samples from the same session within one partition. The benchmark defines allowed inputs, deterministic label mappings, fixed training/validation/test partitions, and task-wise scoring rules. We evaluate majority-class, random-forest, and ET-BERT baselines, an unadapted 27B language model, and independently trained task-specific LoRA adapters on a shared frozen base. Adapters are selected using validation data and evaluated on the corresponding test sets. Task-specific adaptation improves classification performance, supporting instruction tuning across diverse traffic-analysis tasks.

title: Do Agents Still Follow the Rules? Benchmarking Rule Compliance under Agent Context Compaction
summary: LLM agents compact long histories to fit their context windows, but the compacted context must still carry the operating rules that govern later actions. Prior work shows that violations rise after compaction, but measures compliance outside a complete agent harness and does not identify where each violation comes from. We introduce ARCBench(Agent Rule Compliance Benchmark), a configurable benchmark built on the open-source pi agent harness. Its tool-calling agent loop lets us measure rule compliance from actions taken during execution, bringing the evaluation closer to deployed agent workflows. Using ARCBench, we examine where violations after compaction come from, and how different compaction configurations and adversarial settings change their sources. We find that compaction rarely deletes the rule: most violations after compaction occur while the rule is still in the compacted history, with the agent treating a later request as permission, ignoring the rule, and proceeding anyway. Where violations come from depends on the configuration: how the rule is delivered decides whether the agent would break it even without compaction, while the compaction strategy and budget decide whether the rule survives. The strongest compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting the rule in the summary and changing how the agents behave, whereas the strongest defense restores the rule in most summary but still violates. Finally, retaining a rule does not guarantee compliance: compacted runs that retain the rule violate more than twice as often as runs with the full history.

title: Toward Deployable Hardware Roots of Trust for Edge AI: Software PUFs and Their Trade-offs
summary: Deploying AI at the edge increases the need for security features on existing devices. When physical access to the device is available, storing secret keys in non-volatile memory is vulnerable. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) address this by exploiting the unique yet repeatable characteristics of each device, but conventional implementations require design-stage modifications, making them inapplicable to a vast number of existing devices already manufactured. Recently, software PUFs have emerged as an alternative approach, leveraging analog characteristics exposed through software-only interfaces to derive unique responses, without post-fabrication changes. Since edge AI hardware is bound to long operational lifespans, this offers clear economic and engineering value. Existing research on software PUFs remains fragmented. It lacks a holistic review of the trade-offs among choices of components used as entropy sources and software methods to expose analog characteristics. This gap hinders assessing feasibility, comparing approaches, and identifying open challenges towards a hardware root of trust in existing devices. This paper surveys 37 existing software PUF works and compares them against the requirements of on-device model protection: boot-time versus runtime key derivation, and response latency. It analyzes trade-offs, outlines four key challenges that current software PUFs face for edge AI deployment, and highlights promising directions for overcoming barriers to real-world adoption.

title: An Information Hierarchy of Privacy Filters and Odometers
summary:
In sequential data analysis, privacy loss accumulates over time, and privacy filters and odometers are used to control and track this cumulative cost. We study how the information used by differential privacy filters and odometers fundamentally limits what they can achieve. We formalise three levels of information: spec-level information, fixed prior to the interaction; mechanism-level information, which includes the mechanisms instantiated during the interaction; and realisation-level information, which further includes the realised interaction. We classify privacy filters and odometers by the least informative level sufficient to determine their behaviour.
  Our main results establish strict and arbitrarily large separations in achievable performance across this information hierarchy. For privacy filters, moving up the hierarchy can yield an unbounded utility advantage, quantified by a clipped measure of the number of allowed releases. For privacy odometers, it can yield an arbitrarily large improvement in precision, quantified by the expected peak excess of the reported bound over the realised privacy loss. Further, although the information classes are distinct, we show that moving to a richer class need incur essentially no loss in performance.
  Finally, we show that randomisation provides a resource orthogonal to information: at every information level, it can yield an arbitrarily large utility improvement over deterministic filters. Thus, information access and randomisation can be viewed as fundamental resources governing privacy procedures in adaptive interactions.

title: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision
summary: Restricting what a model can say is often mistaken for restricting an attacker's influence over its decision. An attacker can add text to the evidence and steer the model toward a wrong answer that still belongs to the allowed set. We evaluate seven decision models spanning hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). We present Slot Attack, a black-box attack designed for decision models that appends text assembled from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-selected incorrect option. The method relies solely on returned label probabilities, achieves success rates of 32--99\% on initially correct decisions, and identifies the effective component combinations with a median of 17--72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal this vulnerability. Models with near-identical accuracy on the sampled tasks differ by about 20\%age points in attack success. We demonstrate that an attacker can force not just one wrong answer but every available one: on about 20\% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77\% for gpt-6-luna and 98\% for GLiNER2.5; a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out. A fixed answer set constrains a decision's form, not its source; robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.

title: Systematic Derivation of Leakage in Massey Secret Sharing Schemes
summary: Leakage attacks on secret sharing schemes can be based on the exploitation of partial information about individual shares to recover the underlying secret. In coding theory, linear exact repair schemes (LERSs) allow the recovery of a codeword symbol from limited information obtained from the remaining symbols. When applied to code-based secret sharing schemes, such repair schemes can be interpreted as recovering the secret from partial information about the shares, expressed in terms of subfield symbols. Guruswami and Wootters introduced the first explicit constructions of LERSs for low-rate Reed--Solomon codes that is optimal in terms of bandwidth. In this work, we first investigate the construction and algebraic properties of LERSs, building on the Guruswami-Wootters construction. We derive new explicit repair schemes from their construction and establish structural properties of the resulting schemes. Second, we further develop a systematic computational approach based on a Gr{ö}bner bases approach to identify leakage functions associated with LERSs for arbitrary linear codes. This approach enables us to investigate the existence and structural properties of LERSs across different code families and parameter ranges. We first applied our method to Reed-Solomon codes, which gave as further insights into the algebraic structure of LERSs. Moreover, by applying our method to generalized Reed-Muller and Tamo-Barg codes, we identify several LERSs that, to the best of our knowledge, have not previously been described in the literature.

title: Cyber-JEV: Matched Contrastive Fine-Tuning of Language Models for Fast Source-Code Vulnerability Triage
summary: Single-pass scoring models such as Jev give each code function a vulnerability probability, so that security teams can rank many functions for review without generating written explanations. Training an open-weight model for this task is limited by data. Benchmarks with both vulnerable and non-vulnerable labels keep few vulnerable functions once examples related to the test data are removed, while larger public vulnerability records mostly contain vulnerable functions only. Mixing the two lets the data source predict the label, and training on the labeled data alone leaves a model that often scores a fixed function above its vulnerable original. We present Cyber-JEV, a fine-tuning method that uses fix commits to turn these records into comparison groups. Each group holds a vulnerable function, its patched version and up to two unchanged functions from the same file, so the model sees the change that removed a recorded defect. One shared model learns two tasks: classifying functions from the labeled reference data, and ranking the vulnerable function above the other members of its group. At test time the input is one function and the output is a vulnerability score. On a test benchmark of 7,270 functions, an ensemble of five fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B models reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.814, compared with 0.743 for Jev 1.13. With the 4,031 alerts of Jev as the review budget, it misses 16 of 322 vulnerable functions instead of 39. Compared with training on the reference data alone, it ranks the vulnerable version above the patched version 14.8 to 29.2 percentage points more often on three sets of real fixes. Such scores can order the changed functions of a pull request or a release for review under a fixed budget.

title: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for empowering search agents to tackle complex information-seeking tasks. However, since acquiring external information necessitates web search, these agents are highly susceptible to various adversarial attacks (e.g., malicious information injection or stealthy context manipulation). Existing attack strategies inevitably rely on static and human-crafted templates, failing to emulate the dynamic and complex nature of real-world threats. In this paper, we propose an adversarial self-evolution framework that integrates bi-level optimization between the attacker's strategy evolution and the defender's adaptive mitigation, to expose the vulnerabilities of search agents. Specifically, we introduce the Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method to drive the directional evolution of the attack strategy population via contrastive evolutionary signals. To provide a stable environment for this continuous evolution, we further construct a controlled sandbox and design fine-grained metrics to quantify internal vulnerabilities. Extensive experiments across various multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs demonstrate that the proposed framework yields attack efficacy superior to static baselines, underscoring the urgent need to develop more robust defense frameworks.

title: Leakage-Aware Encrypted Semantic Communication with Key-Conditioned Signal Perturbation
summary: Encrypted semantic communication systems protect transmitted messages by inserting key-conditioned modules into a deep-learning semantic communication pipeline, but existing designs rely on a fixed adversarial weight and operate mainly at the semantic-feature level. We propose two changes to the encrypted semantic communication system (ESCS): a key-conditioned signal-domain perturbation layer, called learned adversarial perturbation injection (LAPI), and an information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE)-guided adaptive training rule that {adds an adaptive leakage penalty alongside the fixed adversarial objective} using an InfoNCE-based proxy for mutual information leakage. Experiments on the Europarl corpus over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Rayleigh fading channels show that InfoNCE-guided training is the primary source of eavesdropper suppression, reducing the eavesdropper's bilingual evaluation understudy (BLEU) score to approximately 0.07 at high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Adding LAPI to the InfoNCE-guided objective further lowers the InfoNCE-estimated leakage by 5-9% with low measured inference overhead, while its impact on legitimate-receiver BLEU depends on channel conditions. The two mechanisms operate on different parts of the pipeline and can be jointly applied.

title: Evaluating autonomous self-healing against persistent cyber-attacks
summary: The need for autonomous cyber resilience (ACR) is strongly accelerating. The boost in cyber capabilities of advanced AI is speeding up the attacker-defender rat race to an unprecedented pace. As a result, the field of ACR must progress from early design and experimentation to hands-on evaluation and deployment. To illustrate what is needed for this transition, we put TNO's autonomous immune system-inspired Self-Healing for Cyber Security (SH4CS) software to the test. Our analytic and experimental evaluation results demonstrate that effective cyber resilience is achieved with SH4CS for (repeated) web application vulnerability exploits. Remaining challenges of SH4CS revolve around finding the right balance between predictable resilient behaviour, and adaptiveness to the large variety of cyber threats and applications-to-be-protected.

title: Rethinking Neural Decompilation: Candidate Selection as the Hidden Bottleneck
summary: Reverse engineering obfuscated binaries is a core task in malware analysis and software security auditing. While neural decompilers based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved the readability and functional fidelity of recovered code over heuristic tools such as Ghidra and IDA Pro, a substantial gap remains between best-sample performance and practical single-output accuracy, particularly under code obfuscation. We study this gap through the lens of candidate generation and candidate selection. Using the LLM4Decompile architecture, we show that ground-truth tokens lie within the model's top-five next-token predictions in 95.6% of positions on average and that multi-sample decoding reaches a pass@100 of 93% on HumanEval-Decompile, indicating that correct reconstructions are typically already present in the model's sampling space. We then evaluate a generate-then-select pipeline that ranks 100 candidates per input with text-, syntax-, embedding-, consensus-, and likelihood-based selectors. Negative perplexity emerges as the strongest static selector on HumanEval-Decompile (73.3% pass@1), while execution-guided selection nearly closes the oracle gap on ExeBench (86.3% pass@1). Combined with one epoch of fine-tuning on our newly released ExeBench-Obfuscated dataset containing 362,647 obfuscated OLLVM samples, the same pipeline increases the pass@1 rate for obfuscated binaries to 88.8%, directly contradicting prior claims that released LLM4Decompile checkpoints are unsuitable for obfuscated inputs.

title: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering
summary: Third-party LoRA adapters introduce serious backdoor risks: malicious adapters can maintain normal task performance while embedding hidden, trigger-activated behaviors, making them difficult to detect through standard utility evaluations. Existing removal-based defenses typically sanitize backdoored models by updating, pruning, distilling, or mixing model parameters. However, these approaches are misaligned with adapter-based deployment, where the trusted base model is expected to remain frozen. In this work, we propose LoRA-Patch, a lightweight backdoor defense tailored to LoRA adapters. Our key insight is that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of a poisoned adapter relative to its trusted base model. Building on this insight, LoRA-Patch suppresses trigger-activated behaviors by realigning adapter directions through layer-wise steering, without modifying the base model weights. Extensive experiments across five backdoor attacks and three models show that LoRA-Patch effectively mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforming existing baselines while preserving benign task performance. Moreover, LoRA-Patch is computationally efficient, constructing patches within 20 seconds across all evaluated models and adapters. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/FOXVEDA/LoRA-Patch.

title: Movable Antenna-Assisted Secret Key Generation over Temporally Correlated Channels
summary: Physical-layer key generation (PLKG) exploits reciprocal channel dynamics to generate symmetric keys, addressing the key distribution problem in wireless communications. However, strong temporal correlation in slow-fading environments limits fresh randomness and results in low key generation rates. Movable antennas (MAs) introduce spatial degrees of freedom through antenna repositioning, providing a new approach to addressing the limitation. This paper investigates MA-assisted PLKG over temporally correlated channels. A first-order Gauss-Markov process is utilized to characterize the temporal correlation of multipath gains. We characterize the full-sequence mutual information (MI) over temporally correlated channels. For fixed antenna positions and beamforming, we establish a finite-horizon approximation error bound that vanishes as both effective signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) increase. We derive a closed-form expression for the one-step conditional MI and adopt it as a tractable key-information metric. A nonconvex problem is formulated to jointly optimize antenna positions and per-slot beamforming under transmit-power and minimum-spacing constraints. We develop an alternating optimization algorithm, combining an exact principal-eigenvector beamforming solution with feasible SCA-based projected gradient position updates. Simulation results demonstrate that the MA-assisted scheme outperforms the fixed-position antenna baseline. At a high temporal correlation coefficient, position optimization achieves approximately $51\%$ higher rates than fixed antennas. Joint position and beamforming optimization provides a further $106\%$ gain over position optimization alone, demonstrating more pronounced gains under strong temporal correlation.

title: ATrust: Adaptive Trust Boundary Expansion for Securing LLM Agents
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents take on more complex tasks with greater autonomy, security has become a major obstacle to their broader deployment. Unlike in attacks that require complex exploitation of operating system vulnerabilities, attackers can easily hijack agents through indirect prompt injection (IPI), leading to privacy leakage, financial loss, and destructive operations. However, existing defenses often make security decisions based on limited static trusted evidence or assess observations in isolation. Such rigid trust assumptions can cause task-essential information to be unnecessarily discarded, resulting in over-defense and degraded agent functionality. To address this problem, we propose ATrust, a defense mechanism that adaptively expands the trust boundary during agent runtime. Starting from the user query as the root trust anchor, ATrust evaluates external observations against the current trust boundary and execution state, progressively admitting task-essential information as new trust anchors. This preserves necessary environmental feedback while excluding irrelevant content, whether benign or malicious, from subsequent decision-making, thereby limiting unnecessary exposure to external environment. We evaluate ATrust on AgentDojo and AgentDyn, where it achieves the strongest overall security--utility trade-off among existing defenses. With GPT-4o as the engine model, ATrust reduces the attack success rate on AgentDyn from 37.80% to 4.37% while enhancing utility by 10.00%, outperforming AuthGraph, the state-of-the-art defense, by 12.33%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of ATrust.

title: The Customer Never Sees the Goal: Measuring and Detecting Vulnerability-Targeted Manipulation in LLM Assistants
summary: Companies deploy large language model (LLM) assistants on their websites to advise customers. For commercial reasons, the operator can give an assistant a goal that the customer never sees. This paper focuses on operator-induced vulnerability-targeted manipulation (VTM), in which an assistant pursues such a goal by exploiting a vulnerability the customer discloses. While existing research mainly measures how manipulative a model is, we go further and ask whether VTM can be detected from the customer-AI conversation. To investigate this at scale, we introduce GAP (Goal-Anchored Probing). GAP first records the option a model recommends without any goal and then sets the other option as the operator's goal. We apply GAP to 15 open- and closed-source LLMs and collect 619,600 labeled replies across 540 everyday scenarios in 12 domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) Do assistants with an operator goal target vulnerable customers? (2) Can VTM be detected from the customer-AI conversation? (3) Does detection generalize to unseen models, vulnerabilities, and instruction styles? We first find that 14 of 15 models push the operator goal, and 12 of them use disclosed distress or financial strain to support it. Next, we show that fine-tuned detectors identify exploitative pushes with 79\% accuracy from the reply alone, while zero-shot LLM judges average at most 62\%. Finally, detection weakens on vulnerabilities absent from training. Telling whether a push comes from the operator also becomes unreliable when the assistant is told to hide its goal. We will release our dataset and code to facilitate future research on auditing LLM assistants.

title: Where Does MCP Security End? A Three-Tier Mitigation Mapping Framework for the OWASP MCP Top 10
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become a leading standard for connecting Large Language Models (LLMs) to external tools, software, and data sources. MCP architecture favors ease of integration over security, blending the data and control planes into a single natural language channel. This introduces confused deputy and prompt injection vulnerabilities that cannot be completely mitigated in the software development lifecycle (SDLC) of an MCP server. Structured security guidance for server developers has been outpaced by this adoption trend, leaving them without a clear way to identify where vulnerabilities can be addressed at the server layer and where architectural constraints create hard limits. This paper presents a framework based on OWASP MCP Top 10 mapped to three architectural tiers, developed using Design Science Research (DSR). Vulnerabilities are classified as server-primary, gateway-primary, or protocol-primary applying a cascading decision tree following four questions, resulting in reproducible tier assignments and confidence levels independent of who applies it. The framework was validated against an enterprise-grade Managed File Transfer (MFT) MCP server built in Go. Validation results showed that high-confidence server-tier controls worked as predicted, and low-confidence protocol-tier controls failed for architectural reasons beyond server implementation. The architectural ceiling encountered during practical validation is the main contribution and shows how secure-by-design development can reduce the MCP attack surface but not completely mitigate it.

title: StateFence: Task-State Protection Against Evidence-Chain Contamination in Blue-Team LLM Agents
summary: Indirect prompt injection creates a distinctive risk for blue-team Large Language Model (LLM) agents in Security Operations Centers (SOCs). Malicious instructions can be embedded in telemetry, tickets, retrieval results, or memory and then propagate through alert triage, incident summarization, response recommendation, and Indicator of Compromise (IOC) extraction as locally plausible intermediate decisions. We characterize this failure mode as evidence-chain contamination of protected task state. The main challenge is task dependent: a suspicious string may be malicious control text for summarization but essential evidence for IOC extraction. To address this challenge, we propose StateFence, a task-aware evaluation and defense framework that treats severity labels, incident narratives, response policies, and IOC sets as protected states. StateFence maps indirect prompt-injection attacks into explicit, stealth, multi-hop, and persistent SOC evidence attacks, records observable propagation traces, and routes defenses according to the attacked state. Across controlled SOC cases and public-SOC validation cases, StateFence lowers attack success and reduces failures that appear only after evidence is poisoned, while preserving task utility and avoiding the indicator loss caused by task-mismatched filtering. Our findings indicate that robust blue-team LLM agents require mechanisms that preserve task-critical state under untrusted evidence.

title: Explicit permutations of $(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^m$ with uniformly bounded differential uniformity
summary: Symmetric primitives over Galois rings need nonlinear components whose differentials with respect to ring addition are controlled. Let $R=\mathrm{GR}(4,m)$ and $q=2^m$, so that $(R,+)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^m$ has order $N=q^2$. For every $m\ge1$ we construct an explicit permutation $G_c$ of $R$ all of whose differentials with a nonzero input difference have probability at most $36/N$, whereas every permutation polynomial of $R$ has such a differential of probability at least $2/\sqrt{N}$ (Ronjom--Sandrib). The bound holds for the fixed permutation itself, not on average over keys. Equivalently, $Δ(G_c)\le36$ against $Δ\ge2\sqrt{N}$ for permutation polynomials; since every permutation has $Δ\ge2$, the least differential uniformity of a permutation of $(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^m$ lies between $2$ and $36$ for every $m$. In Teichmuller digits $(a,b)\in\mathbb{F}_q^2$ and for $c\in\mathbb{F}_q$ of absolute trace $1$, $G_c(a,b)=(L,(L^2+L+c)a)$ with $L=(a^2+a+c)b$. The map is $F_c\circ J\circ F_c$, where $F_c(a,b)=(a,(a^2+a+c)b)$ is induced by a polynomial over $R$ and $J$ exchanges the digits: a single digit exchange between two polynomial layers yields a bound independent of $m$. The proof reduces the difference equations, in each of three types of directions, to one-variable polynomials whose degrees do not depend on $m$. For general maps $F\circ J\circ F$ with $F(a,b)=(p(a),h(a)+d(a)b)$, where $p,d,h$ have degrees bounded independently of $m$, $p'\ne0$ and $d$ has no zeros, a Jacobian identity in characteristic $2$ bounds the differentials with nonzero low input and output differences independently of $m$; the remaining directions need a separate argument, which we give for an explicit family ($Δ\le440$, resp. $510$, for odd $m$).

title: When Neither Side Confirms: Destructive Tool Approval Across MCP Servers and Hosts
summary: LLM agents call tools that delete data or move money through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The specification asks for a human who can deny tool calls but splits the mechanism between the server, which can annotate a tool or ask the user through the host (elicitation), and the host application, which decides whether to prompt. We measure both sides from source code. In a 1,000-repository sample of the official MCP registry, an estimated 90% of destructive tools (95% CI 82-95) have no server-side confirmation, and most servers that elicit proceed, or fall back to a flag the model can set, when the host cannot relay the question. Of 41 popular open-source hosts and agent SDKs, 32 have no approval step by default, including 16 of 25 applications. Pairing sampled destructive tools flagged by a rule-based extractor with these applications, 60.7% of pairs have no enforced human approval by default. Through four agent SDKs, four of five low-cost models executed an injected deletion in 479 of 960 runs. If hosts prompted for every tool not annotated read-only or non-destructive, the unapproved share of these pairs would fall to 5.4%; universal elicitation support would leave 56.7%. Applications should therefore configure approval.

title: Ranked but Not Stopped: Detecting Prompt-Injection Hijacks from Typed Decision Models' Output Probabilities
summary: Programs that use a language model as a classifier act on its most probable label. Text injected into the input can move that label to one the attacker chooses, a hijack. A monitor that does not know the attacker's label can read the model's own confidence and raise an alarm when the top probability is low. We test this monitor on AG News topic classification with five systems, three of them served through a provider's API. Pooled over five families of injected text, low confidence ranks hijacked answers above clean ones on four of the five systems (AUROC 0.86-0.90). Ranking them does not stop many of them. A threshold set so that at most 5% of clean answers to separate calibration articles alarm falls among the least confident clean answers, and every more confident hijack passes. In our main gate run on the three API-served systems, the monitor misses 51-70% of the hijacks caused by a plain injected note (per-system point estimates). When the note adds one handwritten sentence that calls the target certain and asks for full probability, the monitor misses 99-100% of the hijacks, although low confidence still ranks them at AUROC 0.70-0.79. Confidence monitors should be tested at their operating alarm rate, against attackers who claim certainty.

title: Networked Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web
summary: Several genuine AI services may repeat one unsupported source, and correcting that source may leave later reports unchanged. We examine these networked consequences of synthetic social engineering (SSE), deliberately misleading influence intended to redirect AI recipients from authorized objectives. Our framework connects social influence, information aggregation, and misinformation correction research to observable evidence and permission boundaries. It separates originating attempts from legitimate intermediaries' work and distinguishes identity, evidentiary support, and authorization. We test four relationships using Qwen3-4B and two briefing tasks across 1,080 research units in our Agent Service Exchange and Evidence Commons (ASE-EC). Multiple dependent publishers produced no supported increase in unsupported verification (78.3% versus 75.0%); publication availability left downstream violation reach at 40.0% in both arms. These comparisons direct attention to weaknesses already present in the reference workflows. High reference error rates and retained private handoffs preclude claims of immunity to social pressure. Without scope revalidation, corrections identifying dependent reports reduced residual invalid decisions from 14.4% to 8.1% at equal notification coverage and increased successful report repairs from 16/63 to 36/63. Scope revalidation added no demonstrated protection, and clearing dialogue offered no established recovery advantage. Unapproved requests persisted, all blocked by an external gateway. For designers, the findings caution against treating publisher count as independent evidence, notification as repair, or cleared histories as recovery. They support targeting corrections at reused reports, assessing factual and permission recovery separately, and enforcing authorization at execution.

title: Fixed Detectors, Moving Code: How Well Do Static Security Analyzers Hold Up over a Decade of C/C++ Evolution?
summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools are often deployed on the assumption that detectors configured today will remain effective on future code, including previously unknown vulnerabilities. We test this assumption using 20,000 vulnerable and fixed C/C++ cases from 1,116 open-source projects (2016-2025), evaluated with three CodeQL releases, three Infer releases, and one Semgrep configuration. To distinguish temporal effects from shifts in code composition, we compare yearly populations, project- and label-matched year pairs, and within-project trajectories. We investigate the largest within-project declines through repair diffs, detection predicates, alert locations, and execution logs, while accounting for failed, degraded, and costly analyses. Under changed-file case-label scoring, overall F1 ranges from 0.066 to 0.478, but count-based AUROC stays near chance (0.495-0.526). Newer CodeQL releases attain higher F1 alongside nearly parallel rises in recall and false-positive rate, not stronger separation of vulnerable from fixed cases. In project-matched year pairs, CodeQL R2024 has negative mean later-minus-earlier F1 at every source-year gap, whereas Infer v1.1 and v1.3 have positive means throughout. Among selected drops, only 6 of 39 CodeQL and 2 of 620 Infer findings overlap a changed repair line. For Semgrep, 78.96% of cases show parser or timeout diagnostics even though every run reports success. These results suggest that apparent changes in temporal SAST effectiveness can arise from broader alerting, changing analysis coverage, and incidental findings, not solely from losses in vulnerability detection. Evaluations of temporal sustainability should fix detector conditions, control for projects, inspect repair-level evidence, and report failed or degraded analyses.

title: Malware Clustering in the Wild: Taxonomy, Challenges, and Evaluation Metrics
summary: As malware continues to grow in volume, diversity, and sophistication, clustering has emerged as a critical technique for analyzing large malware corpora. Clustering enables the discovery of structural relationships, behavioral patterns, and evolutionary trends, and is widely used to group unknown samples, infer malware family boundaries, and identify novel variants. However, existing research remains fragmented, employing a wide range of clustering techniques with no unified perspective that systematically organizes prior work or clearly identifies gaps in the literature. This survey addresses this gap by organizing previous malware clustering research into seven categories: centroid-based, hierarchical-based, density-based, distribution-based, mixed- type, fuzzy, and AI-driven approaches. In addition, this survey summarizes publicly available malware datasets commonly used in clustering research and examines the feature representations derived from these datasets. Our goal is to clarify the current landscape and outline promising avenues for future research on malware clustering, including how AI-driven methods may shape large-scale and reproducible analysis.

title: High-Throughput Private Information Retrieval with on-CPU Accelerators
summary: Private information retrieval (PIR) hides which record a client retrieves by scanning the entire database, and batching is an effective technique to improve throughput by sharing this scan across queries. However, existing CPU-based solutions gain little from batching because each query still requires its own multiplications, and vector instructions perform only a few at a time. GPUs and other discrete accelerators can accelerate these computations, but require extra hardware and can constrain database size due to their limited memory capacity. In this paper, we present AltoPIR, the first PIR system that leverages on-CPU matrix accelerators such as Intel AMX. AltoPIR keeps the accelerator fed from the CPU caches, reading each database byte from memory once for all queries in a batch and never writing intermediate products to memory. This enables high-performance PIR through efficient batching without requiring discrete accelerators. Our evaluation shows that AltoPIR achieves up to 50.1x higher throughput than existing CPU-based solutions and serves databases larger than a GPU's memory.

title: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
summary: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

title: Detect, Repair and Audit: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Defense Against Adversarial Attacks in Energy Forecasting
summary: Accurate electricity-demand forecasting is essential for the modern energy infrastructure. Recently, Times-Series Large Language Models (TS-LLMs) have emerged as a promising approach to forecasting more accurate demand from historical consumption data in zero- and few-shot settings, helping energy operators effectively plan supply and allocate energy resources. However, these models are vulnerable to compromised sensor inputs that can distort forecasts and lead to erroneous market orders or unnecessary load shedding. Existing defenses focus primarily on end-device forecasting, overlooking the distinct data-drift, latency, and audit requirements across energy infrastructure. To address this gap, we extract from major energy standards and regulatory frameworks a three-layer conceptual model that captures the security postures for each layer. Guided by this model, we develop a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) detector coupled with signal repair at local control centers, designed to mitigate distributional data drift through complementary feature-based detection and clean-reference-calibrated repair while meeting latency budgets. We further deploy an evidence-grounded LLM auditing agent with human-in-the-loop validation for audit-critical Virtual Power Plants (VPPs). In our evaluation, the best MARL configuration achieves an F1 score above 0.91 across all dataset-attack pairs, while signal repair reduces adversarial-to-clean input Relative Squared Error (RSE) by up to 83%. The few-shot auditor detects 77.78% of attacks in the Sherlock dataset. On the evaluated hardware, detection and repair require 7.95 ms on average, with a worst-observed latency of 14.50 ms, remaining within the local-center latency budget informed by IEEE 1646.

title: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level
summary: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission measures three-dimensional forest structure with a LiDAR aboard the International Space Station. GEDI observations have geolocation errors of about 10 m, which cause misalignment with other remote sensing data and reduce the accuracy of downstream tasks. Matching GEDI ground elevations against high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) from airborne LiDAR is one way to correct these errors, but such DTMs exist in few regions. To widen this method's applicability, we super-resolved a more widely available low-resolution DTM and used it for the matching. Our question is whether a super-resolved DTM yields the same correction as a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR DTM and, if not, why. In steep forests of western Japan, we super-resolved an existing 10 m-resolution DTM to 1 m. Improving its accuracy required fusion with a global 30 m-resolution DTM from a different source. Using the resulting DTM, we corrected GEDI observation positions first by a single shift per ground track, then per observation. For most tracks, the shifts nearly matched those from the airborne LiDAR DTM, likely because DTM errors canceled out across many observations. Per-observation corrections, however, did not match. At a single observation, the error does not cancel out and is too large for the correction. This error likely originates mainly from the input DTM. Therefore, even without a 1 m-resolution DTM, a roughly 10 m-resolution DTM, fused with a global DTM and super-resolved to 1 m, should yield track-wise corrections nearly matching those from a 1 m-resolution DTM.

title: AdaptivePnP: Fast Auto-Tuned Plug-and-Play for Deconvolution
summary: Plug-and-play (PnP) methods reconstruct images by alternating a data-fitting step with an image denoiser. Their performance depends on two parameters: the step size $γ$ and the measurement noise level $σ$. In practice, $γ$ is often tuned by grid search over validation images and must be retuned whenever the problem setting changes, and $σ$ is assumed known or estimated separately. We propose AdaptivePnP, a PnP framework that jointly estimates $σ$ and $γ$ at every iteration from the data-fitting residual. To do so, we apply the PnP virtual model to the data-fitting proximal map and show that the residual is zero-mean Gaussian with covariance parameterized by $γ$ and $σ$. However, when one parameter is much larger than the other, the residual carries little information about the smaller one and using the maximum likelihood (ML) estimator can degrade the PnP iterations. We therefore introduce the identifiable maximum likelihood (IML) estimator, which restricts the ML estimator to an identifiable window in which the normalized Cramér--Rao bound of every parameter is bounded by a user-specified tolerance. For the virtual model, this window is an interval of ratios $ρ= γ/σ$, so computing the IML estimate reduces to a one-dimensional search over $ρ$. We apply AdaptivePnP to two standard PnP methods, yielding algorithms that require neither a tuned $γ$ nor a known $σ$. On image deblurring and super-resolution, AdaptivePnP matches or outperforms PnP baselines tuned with the true $σ$. Code is available at https://github.com/hdubasullivan/AdaptivePnP.

title: Tomographic Sparse View Selection using the View Covariance Loss
summary: Standard computed tomography (CT) reconstruction algorithms such as filtered back projection (FBP) and Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) require many views for producing high-quality reconstructions, which can slow image acquisition and increase cost in non-destructive evaluation (NDE) applications. Over the past 20 years, a variety of methods have been developed for computing high-quality CT reconstructions from sparse views. However, the problem of how to select the best views for CT reconstruction remains open. In this paper, we present a novel view covariance loss (VCL) function that measures the joint information of a set of views by approximating the normalized mean squared error (NMSE) of the reconstruction. We present fast algorithms for computing the VCL along with an algorithm for selecting a subset of views that approximately minimizes its value. Our experiments on simulated and measured data indicate that for a fixed number of views our proposed view covariance loss selection (VCLS) algorithm results in reconstructions with lower NRMSE, fewer artifacts, and greater accuracy than current alternative approaches.

title: Beyond Segmentation: Enriching ImageCAS with Coronary Ostia Landmarks, Rooted Centerline Graphs, and Open-Weight Localization Models
summary: Coronary ostia and centerlines are key reference points for automated analysis of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA), from surgical planning to intraoperative vessel tracking. However, the only public ostium annotations cover 77 non-gated aortic scans, not CCTA, while CAT08 and ASOCA (32 and 40 CCTA scans) mark the ostia only implicitly, as centerline start points. This work enriches ImageCAS, the largest public dataset for coronary artery segmentation, with ostium annotations for its 1000 patients and centerline graphs rooted at these new ostia, making it, to the authors' knowledge, the largest public dataset for ostium localization and the only one with centerlines following the official ImageCAS masks and starting at annotated ostia. Three annotators marked each ostium in the first 500 volumes; in the next 500, the candidates of a model trained on the first batch were corrected (human-in-the-loop). Six 3D localization models, trained on ImageCAS, CAT08 and ASOCA, were benchmarked on 58 held-out volumes (50 ImageCAS, 4 CAT08, 4 ASOCA). SwinUNETR-V2 and nnResUNet localized all ostia without failure (>5 mm error), with median errors of 0.70-0.87 mm. Trained on CAT08 and ASOCA alone, SwinUNETR-V2 fails on 34% of right and 53% of left ostia, whereas adding 250 ImageCAS volumes removes all failures. The centerlines were extracted by a deterministic, quality-controlled minimal-path procedure; on ASOCA, they cover a median of 99.5% of the reference length, with a median per-patient mean distance of 0.22 mm between matched reference points and centerlines. Annotations, centerlines, code, and weights are available at https://hal9000-lab.github.io/.

title: SmartBloch-Agent: An Agentic Framework for Automated MRI Sequence Design and Optimization
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow.
